newsitem.title: GERMANY: Merrill sees German overheating risks - paper.
newsitem.headline: Merrill sees German overheating risks - paper.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch sees a risk of overheating in the German economy due to the weaker mark and the impact of loose monetary and fiscal policies before EMU, a German newspaper said on Sunday.

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said Merrill Lynch's "Deutscher Monitor" analysis of the German economy, to be published on Monday, would also warn investors that political risks were returning to the German financial markets.

The newspaper said Merrill analysts forecast that as a result of the weaker mark, an expected loosening of Bonn budgets from 1998, a relaxed monetary policy, and the threat of higher wage cost pressure, there could be "serious inflationary dangers" from next year.
It said the investment house forecast that inflation would be at around 1.6 percent in the current year but could rise to as much as 2.5 percent in 1998.
It added that in the next 18 months, as Germany prepares to join the single European currency in 1999, "the toughest decisions in Germany since reunification will have to be made".
"Investors should as a result grasp the fact that political risks are returning to the German financial markets".

As evidence that the Bundesbank had turned away from a monetary policy traditionally perceived as strict, Merrill cited the bank's decision last year to lower the interest rate governing securities repurchase agreements to three percent.
"Our own econometric studies show that, had the Bundesbank been sticking to its previous course, it should not have lowered its repo rate to a record low of three percent last August," it said.
The so-called repo rate is one of the most closely watched of all the Bundesbank's interest rates and has remained at three percent since last August.
Merrill forecast that the Bundesbank's support of the single European project would mean it would tend to a "continuing loose" monetary policy.
